kjv-italics-revision: The King James Bible prints some words in italics. Those are words the 1611 translators added to make the English read smoothly. They have no equivalent in the Hebrew, and they exist only in that printed edition. David Wright showed that a conservative 22 to 38 percent of all Book of Mormon Isaiah differences from the King James occur at or around those italic words. About 40 percent of the italic words are simply dropped. No one translating from ancient plates could know which English words a seventeenth-century committee had supplied.
deutero-isaiah-problem: Since the late 1700s, critical scholarship has held that Isaiah 40-55 was written by an unnamed author during the exile, around 545 to 539 BC. The reasons are cumulative — the language, the history, and the theology. Those chapters assume the Babylonian exile is already happening, and they name Cyrus, a Persian king not yet born in Isaiah's day. Chapters 56-66 are dated later still. Lehi left Jerusalem around 600 BC. Yet Nephi, Jacob and Abinadi all quote those chapters at length, and Abinadi builds an entire sermon on Isaiah 53.
another-gospel-canon-closure: Two arguments get made together, and only one of them works. The first says the Book of Mormon is "another gospel" under Paul's warning in Galatians 1:8, where even an angel from heaven preaching a different gospel is accursed — which critics apply straight to the angel Moroni. The second says adding to scripture breaks the closing warnings of Revelation 22:18-19 and Deuteronomy 4:2. Whether the first lands depends entirely on whether the gospel content actually differs, which is what the doctrinal cases on this site examine.
grace-after-all-we-can-do: 2 Nephi 25:23 says "it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do." Moroni 10:32 adds that you must deny yourself of all ungodliness, and then his grace is sufficient. Critics read both as making grace conditional on human effort first. The Bible says the opposite in Ephesians 2:8-9 — saved by grace through faith, and not of works, so that no one can boast. The disagreement is not about whether obedience matters. It is about whether it is the ground of salvation or the fruit of it.
trinitarian-monotheism-1830: The Book of Mormon teaches strict monotheism, and its Father-Son unity is so tight that it reads as trinitarian or even modalist. Mosiah 15:1-5 says Christ is "the Father, because he was conceived by the power of God" and is "the Father and the Son… one God." Alma 11:26-29 states there is one God and no other. Alma 11:38-39 calls Christ the very Eternal Father. None of the doctrines that define later Mormonism appear anywhere in it — no plurality of gods, no eternal progression, no God with a body, no exaltation of humans.
1837-son-of-edits: In the 1830 first edition, 1 Nephi identified Jesus directly as God. 11:18 called Mary "the mother of God." 11:21 called him "the Lamb of God, yea, even the Eternal Father." 11:32 said "the everlasting God, was judged of the world." 13:40 said "the Lamb of God is the Eternal Father." In the 1837 Kirtland edition Joseph Smith inserted the words "the Son of" into each one. The change is small, deliberate, and lands in the same years his teaching about God was shifting.
jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132: Jacob 2:24-27 says the many wives and concubines of David and Solomon were "abominable before me, saith the Lord," and commands that no man among you have more than one wife, and no concubines. Doctrine and Covenants 132:38-39 says the opposite. David's wives and concubines "were given unto him of me," and he sinned only in the case of Uriah. Solomon is listed among those who sinned not. The Bible agrees with the Book of Mormon here, and D&C 132 stands against both.
unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett: Moroni 8:18 says God is "not a partial God, neither a changeable being; but he is unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity." Mormon 9:9-10 and 9:19 say the same. That agrees with the Bible — Psalm 90:2, Malachi 3:6, and Isaiah 43:10, where God says "before me there was no God formed." It contradicts Joseph Smith's King Follett discourse of 1844, which taught that God was once a man like us and dwelt on an earth, and that men may become gods in turn.
no-postmortem-repentance: Alma 34:32-35 teaches that "this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God," and that after it comes "the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed." Those who put off repentance are sealed to the devil, and "this is the final state of the wicked." That agrees with the Bible in Hebrews 9:27 and with the fixed gulf of Luke 16:26. Later teaching added the spirit world, the preaching of the gospel to the dead, and baptism performed by proxy for them.
born-at-jerusalem: Alma 7:10 prophesies that Jesus "shall be born of Mary, at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers." The Bible's prophecy in Micah 5:2 and its fulfilment in Matthew 2:1 and Luke 2:4-7 place the birth in Bethlehem. Critics call it a plain geographical error by Joseph Smith, and note that the Bible he knew made Bethlehem famous. This is one of the weaker criticisms on the site, and the Latter-day Saint reply to it is unusually strong.
plain-precious-things-removed: 1 Nephi 13:26-29 and 13:40 claim that a "great and abominable church" deliberately took from the gospel "many parts which are plain and most precious, and also many covenants," corrupting the Bible after the apostles. That claim is the foundation of the case for a Restoration. It is also testable. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied around 125 BC, matches the medieval Hebrew text with roughly 95 percent verbal identity. The New Testament survives in thousands of copies from too early, too many places, and too many languages for a coordinated removal to go unrecorded.
no-nephite-material-culture: The Book of Mormon describes literate, metal-working, city-building civilizations numbering in the millions, fighting battles with hundreds of thousands of casualties, in the pre-Columbian Americas. After about 190 years of professional archaeology in the Americas, not one city, battlefield, road, temple, artifact or skeleton has been identified with it. No inscription in any related script has been authenticated. And the church itself takes no official position on where any of it happened.
translation-seer-stone: The best-attested account of the translation comes from Emma Smith, David Whitmer and Martin Harris — insiders, not critics. Joseph Smith placed a seer stone in his hat, buried his face in it to block the light, and dictated the English text he saw. The gold plates were often covered, in another room, or not present at all. It was the same stone he had used for treasure-seeking in the 1820s, the practice that brought him before a court in 1826. For about 150 years church manuals and paintings showed him reading from the plates instead.
